We've heard about the marine realm, the freshwater realm, and the terrestrial
realm, but there's also another important one, which is the aerial realm, and that
is what I'm going to talk about. So while we all had, I hope, a good
night's sleep, there were millions of songbirds migrating over
us south. And they do this
mainly at night, and they often do this at very high altitudes
in massive numbers and in a very broad scale.
You have some choke points, but they typically do this in a very broad front
all over the continent. And that makes it difficult to monitor.
You can use citizen science observations, but those are mainly coming from
the birds coming back to the ground to roost, or
you can use GPS trackers, but then you can only track a number of individuals,
and it's also harder with songbirds, which are smaller.
But luckily, we have weather radars, and there is a network of weather
radars that is across the whole continent.
It is monitoring the sky 24/7. And we mainly do this,
meteorological institutes do this, to know
what the weather is going to be like, so to monitor precipitation.
And the way a radar works is it emits a microwave into the sky at
different angles, and they do this up to 35 kilometers from the
radar. And then if an object in the sky, whether it's
rain, snow, dust, or animals,
some of those microwaves are bounced back in all different directions, and some of
those are received back by the radar, which then knows, "Oh, there are
these objects in the sky." So,
this is a very useful tool. What you see here are not all the weather radars in
Europe. There's more. But these are the ones that we have access to.
And why would we want to have access to weather radars?
And that is because, and I think this is so cool, weather radars can actually
detect animals in the sky as well. So this is mainly useful or
applicable for birds. Insects are a lot harder.
Bats, too, unless there's really big roosts coming out
of a cave, for example. Then you can detect those on weather radar.
But what you can see in the image up there,
basically, you have to think of this radar as looking in different angles.
So you see these donut shapes of things that were at different altitude
layers in the sky. And you can differentiate those
from precipitation because the birds
typically have a more variant speed and direction than the rain, which
is typically going into a more uniform direction, and also the
reflectivity of animals in the sky is typically lower than rain
and precipitation. And through that,
through algorithms that were developed by a community, the Volto Bird
algorithm can extract that animal information
from weather radar data. And
we then can know the altitude at which animals were
flying, the speed, the direction, and also
the density or the amount of animals.
You basically translate the reflectivity that you get back into an
average size of a songbird, and then you can apply numbers to
those. These are the amount of birds that were in the sky at this altitude.
What we do not know is species information.
It is basically we know there's meat in the sky.
And through this technology, there's a whole community that has started,
the radar aviary ecology community.
And this group of people is basically using radar to study animals
aloft. And not only through weather radar, but also through more
specialized radars as vertical-looking radars, which are
very local but can detect
very
precise also insects, and sometimes they can also detect through
Doppler effect, the wind beat frequency, which then can be translated into
species groups. Or tracking radars, which are more like the
military radars, but you track animals rather than aircraft, for example.
This community has
been going on for about 10 years and matured and
has developed a number of things, and one of them is just like that is a data
standard. So we have the VPTS CSV file,
or format, which is
a format to express the time series of what we call vertical
profiles. So you have altitude layers of animal
migration, and we use the frictionless table
schemas to define the fields that you can find, which is direction,
speeds, the radar location, and also the types and
constraints of those fields. We also have a similar format to express the
raw polar volume data that is coming from the radar, as well as
we have a list of
the weather radars in Europe and the metadata for those, the status,
which is co-maintained by the meteorological community.
But it's especially important for us that we know if a radar has
changed codes, that it is actually the same radar at the same location, but, for
example, with a new upgrade, so we can build longer time series with codes
that have changed so we can tie those together.
And the other thing we have started in 2017 is a-
Bucket, the Aloft data portal, where we can
store this vertical profile data.
The meteorological institutes have been doing slowly a good job to actually
open up radar data and not only keep it under a license.
But they typically keep this data only for two days, so you only have
access to the data of now and not historical data.
But to be able to do actually real science over a long time period, we
have started to archive the
derived biological data from this weather radar data.
And so this is a
data repository over 24 European countries,
173 radar locations, and we've also filled up the
historical data until 2012.
And this is a time series of almost close to 5,000 days.
So it's a very long time series that we have.
We've also archived this on Zenodo under CC0 license, and the
really cool thing is that this is updated daily.
So as data are coming in, it's also added to this repository,
with a time delay of about one to two days.

So how do we evolve from here? There's a lot of potential here,
there's data there, to something like a digital twin of the aerial
habitat.
And I think the main thing why such a twin would be useful is
migration forecasting, so that you can have models running on the
historical data to be able to predict what kind of migration are we going to
have in the future, which is really useful for bird collision
prevention. So birds often collide with wind
turbines, but also with aircraft, and the first is dangerous for the birds, but the
second can be very dangerous for the passengers of the aircraft as well.
So it is very useful that we can predict when there's going to be massive migration
of birds. And radar is already used for that
for larger birds, but also for passerines, it would be very useful.
The other one would be disease threat modeling. Avian flu, for example.
If you know where
waterfowl is going to move, and we can differentiate that from the radar data,
that would be really useful.
And it's also very cool for public outreach, and it's, I think,
an important essential biodiversity variable, the biomass that is flowing over a
continent.
But the challenges we have is,
for meteorologists, these birds are clutter in the data.
They used to call them angels in World War II.
It's like things that they see on the radar data that cannot really explain.
And it's still the case. Some are interested, but they typically
don't want the biological data and the radar data.
They want the precipitation, and they also have limited funds, so they
tend to filter the data and then only publish the filtered data, while we
want the unfiltered data.
The other thing is the taxonomic information. Well, you don't have much.
It's meat in the sky. But if you combine it with, for example,
citizen science data on the grounds, you are able to know, oh, we had a
huge flux of migration, then you can actually know, oh, and these were suspicious
composition that is very likely to be in there.
And then the typical thing is, this is done by a small community,
so building and maintaining that infrastructure and scaling is a huge
challenge.
In the US, they have a more unified weather radar network.
It's only done by one organization, NOAA.
They've been able to build on the historical data that's also been open longer,
models that can actually predict bird migration.
It's called BirdCast, and users can go there.
This is a picture from the night of September 21, but you can also now
go to 25, 26 of September, so they predict three days ahead.
And you see this flow, this bloom of migration.
So they say, "Yeah, there's going to be about 340 million birds flying over

But that's also when birders know, okay, it's really useful to go
out now, or the next night it's going to be rain, and we predict there's going to

So we hope to get there at some point with the European weather radar as well.
And yeah, I think the take home message for me is
weather radars can detect birds. It is really cool.
We already have a network that is out where we don't need to deploy anything.
The sensors are already out there, and I think it's a
very unique type of data that they capture.
And really, the strength comes from combining this with other digital

1.5 billion animals
on GBIF as a data set. It's
just meat in the sky that doesn't belong on GBIF.
But when combining with other sources, we can do really, really cool things.
